maxim

MAK-sim -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, MAK. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Maxim is a short statement of general truth.

Coach ended every season with the same maxim: 'Play for the name on the front of the jersey, not the back.'

Example

Deciding whether to toss a half-used notebook, Amara hears her grandmother's favorite maxim: 'Waste not, want not.' She keeps the notebook for lists -- and three weeks later is very glad she did.

'Waste not, want not' packs a general truth into four short, memorable words -- compact enough to carry around and apply to new situations. A maxim is a rule of thumb dressed in its best clothes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

adage: An adage is an old saying repeated for so long that people accept it as true -- 'haste makes waste.' A maxim does not need age: it is any short statement of general truth, and a coach or a writer can coin a fresh maxim today.

slogan: A slogan is a short, catchy phrase built to sell or promote something -- a product, a team, a campaign. A maxim claims to state a truth to live by; a slogan only needs to stick in the memory, whether or not it is true at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

falsehood: a statement that is not true

rambling: long, unfocused talk

Where it sits · how broad and time-tested the saying is — motto → maxim → proverb

motto vs. maxim: A motto is personal or institutional -- one team, one family, one school lives by it -- while a maxim claims to state a truth that holds for everyone.

proverb vs. maxim: Proverb is the strongest on tradition: a maxim can be coined yesterday by a coach or a writer, but a proverb has been polished by whole generations repeating it.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — maxim-

root — maxim-: greatest (Latin maximus)

Put it together

Put it together: Maxim comes from the medieval Latin phrase maxima propositio, 'the greatest premise' -- the biggest, most fundamental truth an argument rests on. The phrase shrank to one word, and a maxim is still exactly that: a general truth packed into the smallest possible box.

Use the root in a new word: maximize

Root Check

Word Choice

A maxim is short, quotable, and general: 'measure twice, cut once,' 'slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.' If it names a specific person or event, it is not a maxim -- and if it takes a paragraph, it is advice, not a maxim. People live by maxims, quote them, and tape them above desks.
